title: Building capacity, together.
text:
Teaching
  
    Building capacity, together.
  
  
    Methodological literacy is one of the most empowering things we can give the next generation of urban professionals. My teaching aims to make rigorous spatial thinking accessible, reproducible, and genuinely useful — for designers, planners, and researchers alike.
  




  
    Philosophy
    
      Data as a design tool.
    
    
      The data revolution gave us new instruments — but more importantly, it gave us a new way of thinking. I teach from this premise: that learning to work with spatial data is not a technical skill, it is a cognitive shift that allows designers and planners to engage with complexity at a scale that was previously impossible.
    
    
      Maps are everywhere now. Perhaps there has never been a moment when so many people could read and use a map — to navigate, to understand, to advocate. That is a profound cultural shift, and it carries a responsibility: to teach data literacy as a form of civic and creative power.
    
    
      I also research and teach the role of AI in spatial design education — exploring how computational intelligence can become a design partner, and what new literacies students need to work with it critically and creatively.
    
  
  
    
      Teaching photo
    
  




  
    Platforms & Community
    
      Open methods for open cities.

      Rbanism Community — founding and core member of the open community advancing the use of R in urbanism and spatial research. rbanism.org ↗

Teaching Philosophy
I approach teaching as an act of translation: between disciplines, between methods, and between data and design. I want students to leave my courses not just knowing how to run an analysis, but understanding why it matters and how to communicate what they find.
I am also actively exploring the role of artificial intelligence in spatial and urban design education — not as a shortcut, but as a genuinely new way of engaging with complex urban problems.

  Research Interests & Approach
  How I think about cities
  
    My research sits at the intersection of urbanism, landscape architecture, and spatial data science — with urban resilience and climate adaptation as the central thread. I am drawn to questions about how cities respond to pressure, where they fail, and what kinds of spatial interventions actually make a measurable difference.
    I work predominantly with quantitative methods — GIS, QGIS, R — applying spatial analysis and modeling to understand urban systems and assess the performance of design and planning solutions. What drives me is the belief that better questions and better tools can lead to better cities.
    Lately I have been deeply curious about what artificial intelligence means for how we teach and practice spatial and urban design — not as a shortcut, but as a genuinely new way of engaging with complex spatial problems.
  
  
    ● Now · Active
    I am assembling a new research team and actively looking for collaborators — researchers, doctoral candidates, and practitioners who share a commitment to data-driven approaches to urban resilience. I am also seeking partnerships with municipalities and public organisations. → Get in touch
  




  
  




  Teaching & Community
  Building capacity, together
  
    I believe that methodological literacy is one of the most empowering things we can give to the next generation of urban professionals. At TU Delft, I coordinate the Spatial Data and GIS learning line in the MSc Urbanism programme — making rigorous spatial thinking accessible, reproducible, and genuinely useful for designers and planners.
    I am also a founding and core member of the Rbanism Community — an open initiative advancing the use of R in urbanism and spatial research. Building that community has reinforced something I care about deeply: sharing methods and knowledge across disciplines makes all of our work better.

text:
About
    
      DanieleCannatella
    
    
      Assistant Professor in Urban Data for Design
      Section of Urban Data Science
      Dept. of Urbanism · Faculty of Architecture
      TU Delft, The Netherlands
    
    
      ↓ CV
      Email
      GitHub
    
    
      
      Portrait
    
  

  
    
      I am an Assistant Professor in Urban Data for Design at TU Delft. I work at the intersection of urbanism, landscape architecture, and spatial data science — with urban resilience and climate adaptation as the central thread.
    
    
      My starting point is a conviction: the digital revolution is not a technical revolution — it is a mental one. We gave ourselves augmented tools not to do the same things faster, but to think at a different level of complexity. A complexity that entangles spatial scales from the yard to the planet, and temporal scales from a human lifetime to geological cycles — all in the light of the acceleration that digitalization has brought about.
    
    
      Data are not neutral. They are political — generated by political will, reflecting it, and dictating it.
    
    
      Digital tools let us focus on flows, on spatial interactions decoupled from the concept of proximity, to unpack challenges that were previously too complex to hold: climate change, environmental degradation, and the persistent failure of cities to keep pace with the urgency of adaptation.
    
    
      I also work extensively with AI — exploring what it means for how we teach and practice spatial design, and how computational intelligence might become a genuine design partner rather than a shortcut.
    
  




  
    My Journey
    
      Where it started
    
    
      [Write your personal origin story here — what drew you to urbanism, to spatial data, to resilience as a research focus? What was the turning point or period that shaped your trajectory?]
    
    
      [Continue with your path through disciplines and institutions — the questions that kept coming back, the realisations that shifted your direction.]
    
  
  
    
    
      Photo 1
      Photo 2
      
        "Better questions and better tools lead to better cities."
      
    
  




  
    What I mean by new cities
    
      Just. Livable.Climate-proof. Alive.
    
    
      Designing for climate adaptation carries an imperative: bring nature back into cities. Whether adapting to heat, managing floods, increasing biodiversity, or enabling phytoremediation — the answer points toward landscape. Projects — realized or stuck in a drawer — tell us what we believe, and how we translate those beliefs into spatial form.
    
    
      This is how spatial planners contribute to the re-territorialization of cities (Raffestin): linking them to their surrounding environment, framing them in a global network where relational position has overtaken geographical location. Data-driven approaches can speed up adaptation, lower the costs of analysis, and democratize planning in areas that lack the economic and governance resources to act alone.
    
  




  
    The questions that drive me
    
      
        "What do data tell about ourselves — our beliefs, our values?"
        Data reflect political choices about what gets measured, who gets counted, and what is made visible. Reading data critically is reading power.
      
      
        "How can we design smarter, faster, more systemic adaptation?"
        Automated digital workflows allow replicability and scaling. What takes months of analysis can be reduced to hours — and applied across geographies that lack the resources to act alone.
      
      
        "How can data-driven approaches unlock design creativity?"
        Maps are instruments of discovery. Data allow the creation of infinite maps that reveal spatial patterns, unexpected relationships, and new design hypotheses.
      
      
        "What is the role of AI in spatial design education?"
        Not about automating design — but about what changes when computational intelligence becomes a design partner. What new literacies do students need?
